scripts.title: Book Your Own Room
scripts.spoken_text: You can build a practice that helps a small hotel get its returning guests to book direct, instead of paying a booking site to meet them again. You can run the first piece tonight, on your phone. Pick an independent property near you, twenty to forty rooms. Search for it the way a guest would. Does a free link to the hotel's own site show up beside the site rates? Google shows one for a property connected through a partner, and charges nothing for it. Compare the direct rate to the site's. Try to finish a direct booking yourself. Whatever breaks is your finding. Not findable, not bookable, or a direct rate that costs the guest more. Ten minutes, and you have half an audit.

scripts.title: It Sounds Like Marketing. It's Operations.
scripts.spoken_text: You can build a service that gets a small hotel's returning guests to book direct, instead of paying a booking site to meet them again. It sounds like marketing. The work is operations. At a twenty room inn, the person who would write the thank you is the one checking in a guest and finding a plumber. The direct path is not a system, it is a list of small jobs, and the list belongs to nobody. The drafting got cheap. A language model writes the message, an automation tool schedules it. The judgment did not: who gets one, and what you tell the owner. So the qualification is not hotel marketing. It is owning a list of small recurring jobs in a business you do not own. Rates and revenue management stay outside.

scripts.title: The Guest Book
scripts.spoken_text: You can build a direct-booking practice for small hotels. Get one constraint right before you pick a tool. Booking dot com's own partner help says it does not share private guest email addresses. Both sides see an alias ending at guest dot booking dot com, and partners are asked to keep the conversation on the platform. So you cannot win a guest back from a relay address, and you are not supposed to try. What the inn needs first is not an email tool. It is a guest book of its own, at the front desk, that the guest chooses to sign. The registration card and the wifi login ask for the guest's own email. That list runs under the American email law, and European rules for European guests. Check your jurisdiction. This is not legal advice.

scripts.title: Four Numbers
scripts.spoken_text: You can build a direct-booking practice, and price it honestly off four numbers you ask the owner for. Rooms. Average nightly rate. Occupancy. And the share of bookings arriving through the sites. That gives you the revenue the sites carry. Apply a commission band and you have the annual cost. Then assume a shift in the mix, and say out loud that the size of that shift is a hypothesis nobody has measured. Subtract what running direct costs. What is left is the recoverable amount, a month. That is the ceiling, and your fee lives under it. On an illustrative twenty room inn at a hundred and eighty a night and seventy percent occupancy, it lands near a thousand to fourteen hundred dollars a month. Some properties cannot fund this. The arithmetic tells you which, before you quote.
